props.title: Down with Love

sections.content: Down with Love (2003) brilliantly recreates and satirizes 1960s romantic comedies, particularly the Doris Day-Rock Hudson vehicles like Pillow Talk (1959) and Lover Come Back (1961). Director Peyton Reed meticulously crafts every detail - from the split-screen phone calls to the oversaturated Technicolor palette - while adding modern sensibilities and sexual politics. Ewan McGregor and Renée Zellweger perfectly channel the chemistry and acting styles of Hudson and Day, but with a knowing wink that elevates the film beyond mere pastiche.

sections.content: The film's attention to period detail extends beyond just visual aesthetics. The jazzy score by Marc Shaiman captures the essence of Henry Mancini's work in films like Breakfast at Tiffany's (1961), while the costume design by Daniel Orlandi references the bold fashion statements of films like That Touch of Mink (1962). Even the opening credits sequence, with its geometric animations and split-screen effects, perfectly mimics the work of Saul Bass and other innovative designers of the era.

What sets Down with Love apart is how it subverts the sexual politics of its inspiration material. While maintaining the playful tone of 1960s sex comedies, it comments on gender roles and feminism through Sarah Paulson's character and Zellweger's feminist author Barbara Novak. The film's big third-act reveal cleverly turns the tables on the deception plots common to the genre, making it both a loving homage and modern critique. SUBHEAD: Modern Romantic Comedy Homages

sections.content: Down with Love exists within a tradition of modern films that pay tribute to classic romantic comedies while updating their formulas. Far From Heaven (2002) similarly recreated the look of Douglas Sirk melodramas, while What Women Want (2000) and Miss Congeniality (2000) updated the battle-of-the-sexes workplace comedy for contemporary audiences.
